# Diagnosing Oil-in-Coolant on an Isuzu 6HH1 Engine

When you find oil in the radiator of an Isuzu CUBIC equipped with a 6HH1 engine (8,300cc, 6-cylinder, non-turbo), the system has failed its primary sealing integrity. The specific symptom where no water is found in the crankcase but oil appears in the coolant points to a one-way breach: fluids are moving from the lubrication side into the cooling side, not necessarily back and forth. This directionality helps narrow the root cause immediately.

The 6HH1 is an air-cooled or liquid-cooled diesel unit depending on the specific CUBIC chassis configuration, but in this context, it relies on a robust head gasket or integrated cylinder liner seals to keep these two fluids separate. Finding oil in the radiator indicates that high-pressure combustion gases or lubricating oil have found a path into the coolant reservoir. Since you did not find water in the crankcase, we can likely rule out a massive piston ring failure that would allow significant blow-by to wash down past the rings and accumulate in the sump, though some minor dilution might exist if the engine were run for long periods.

The fact that you have already changed the seals suggests you addressed the most common failure point: the head gasket or the water pump seal. If oil is still present after replacing these components, you must look elsewhere. One critical area to investigate is the oil cooler itself. In many heavy-duty diesel architectures, an oil-to-water heat exchanger is integrated into the engine block or mounted externally. If the internal passages of this cooler are corroded or the core is physically breached, oil will migrate into the coolant regardless of the condition of the head gasket.

Another potential culprit involves the cylinder liner seals on the 6HH1. These engines often utilize wet liners that rely on O-rings for sealing against the coolant jacket. If these specific seals are compromised and you have not yet inspected the mating surface of the block where they sit, debris or improper installation could allow oil to leak into the water galleries. Additionally, check the freeze plugs (core plugs) on the engine block. A failed plug can create a low-resistance path for fluids to mix, especially under thermal expansion cycles.

To verify the extent of contamination, perform a chemical test on the coolant sample. If the specific gravity drops significantly or if emulsification persists after a complete flush and seal replacement, it implies internal corrosion within the oil cooler core rather than just a gasket leak. Replacing the oil cooler is often a necessary trade-off to restore system reliability, even if the primary seals were new.

Finally, consider the thermostat housing and its O-ring. While less common as a source of major oil ingress, a cracked thermostat housing or a failed internal valve can sometimes channel oil from a nearby gallery into the radiator neck if the design allows cross-contamination. Ensure that the coolant system has been thoroughly flushed with an appropriate inhibitor (such as silicate-based or organic acid technology) to remove any acidic byproducts from the oil, which could accelerate corrosion in the remaining metal components.

If you have replaced the head gasket and cylinder liner seals and the issue persists, the oil cooler is the most probable remaining source of failure. Ignoring this can lead to catalytic converter damage due to oil fouling or engine overheating if the coolant flow becomes restricted by sludge.
